blocks.text: Practice long questions for the whole of Chapter 20 (Aromatic Hydrocarbons), in the shape of a Board long question: each theory question carries 4 marks (describe, explain, give equations, draw where needed), and the chapter's numericals are solved step by step. Each question has a full model answer.

blocks.prompt: 1 Describe the development of the structure of benzene from its molecular formula to Kekule's structure. What do X-ray studies show about its shape, bond angles and bond lengths? (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Molecular formula: after its discovery, benzene was found to be C₆H₆, the simplest aromatic hydrocarbon.

Linear structures: some scientists proposed linear structures, but these were soon rejected because they could not explain the properties of benzene.

Kekule's structure (1865): the German professor August Kekule proposed benzene as a six-membered cyclic compound with alternate single and double bonds. It explained many properties of benzene, but it did not fully explain its physical and chemical properties.

X-ray studies:
• Planar molecule, a regular hexagon of six sp² hybridized carbon atoms.
• Each carbon is bonded to three atoms; C–C–C and H–C–C angles are 120°.
• C–H bond length 109 pm (1.090 Å).
• All C–C bonds are equal, 139 pm (1.3970 Å), between the C–C single bond (154 pm) and the C=C double bond (133 pm).

Equal C–C bonds cannot be explained by fixed alternate single and double bonds; they are explained by delocalised π electrons.

book_ref.quote: X-ray studies of benzene exhibits a planar configuration

blocks.prompt: 2 Explain the thermodynamic stability of benzene on the basis of heats of hydrogenation. Define resonance energy and give its value. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Benzene, like alkenes, has double bonds but is much more stable. Evidence comes from heats of hydrogenation, which relate to thermodynamic stability. All the compounds below give cyclohexane, the common low-energy reference point.

• Cyclohexene (one C=C) → cyclohexane: 120 kJ mol⁻¹ released.
• Cyclohexadiene (two C=C) expected: 2 × 120 = 240 kJ mol⁻¹.
• Hypothetical 1,3,5-cyclohexatriene (three C=C) expected: 3 × 120 = 360 kJ mol⁻¹.
• Benzene, actual: only 208 kJ mol⁻¹.

Benzene therefore lies 360 − 208 = 152 kJ mol⁻¹ lower in energy than the hypothetical cyclohexatriene; it is much more stable.

Resonance energy (delocalisation energy): the amount by which the actual heat of hydrogenation of benzene is lower than the theoretical value; for benzene 152 kJ mol⁻¹. It arises because the π electrons are delocalised over the ring through π orbital overlap on all six carbon atoms.

book_ref.quote: Let us analyse the heats of hydrogenation of different cyclohexenes.

blocks.prompt: 3 In a series of measurements, a cyclic alkene with one C=C bond releases 119 kJ mol⁻¹ on hydrogenation, and an aromatic ring compound that would have three such C=C bonds in a Kekule-type structure releases 206 kJ mol⁻¹. Calculate (i) the expected heat of hydrogenation of the Kekule-type structure (ii) the resonance energy (iii) the resonance energy as a percentage of the expected value. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation: Multiply the one-bond value by three for the expected value; the resonance energy is expected minus actual.

book_ref.quote: It shows benzene is much more stable than the hypothetical cyclohexatriene.

steps: Resonance energy = expected − actual = 357 − 206 = 151 kJ mol⁻¹
The actual value is lower, so the compound is more stable than the Kekule-type structure by 151 kJ mol⁻¹

blocks.prompt: 4 Explain the atomic orbital structure of benzene. How does it account for equal C–C bond lengths and the usual symbol of benzene? (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
σ framework:
• Each carbon atom is sp² hybridized.
• Its three sp² orbitals form three σ bonds: two with adjacent carbons (sp²–sp²) and one with hydrogen (sp²–s, using the 1s orbital of H).
• All sp² orbitals are in one plane, so all C and H atoms are coplanar at 120°: a planar hexagon with 12 σ bonds.

π bonding:
• Each carbon has one unhybridized 2p orbital, perpendicular to the σ framework and parallel to the others.
• The six 2p orbitals overlap sideways all round the ring, forming a π-electron cloud above and below the plane; the molecule is conjugated.
• The six π electrons are shared equally by all six carbons: delocalization of π electrons.

Consequences:
• All six C–C bond lengths are the same, 139 pm, between C–C (154 pm) and C=C (133 pm).
• Benzene is drawn as a hexagon with an inscribed circle; the circle represents the delocalized π electrons.
• Delocalization gives extra stability (resonance energy 152 kJ mol⁻¹).

book_ref.quote: The hexagonal frame work of benzene ring can be conveniently explained by using hybridization approach.

blocks.prompt: 5 Describe the rules for naming monosubstituted and disubstituted benzenes, with examples. What are ortho, meta and para positions? (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Monocyclic aromatic hydrocarbons have one benzene ring; polycyclic ones have two or more. Benzene derivatives are named in two styles: with the suffix 'benzene', or by a special name.

Monosubstituted benzenes (one substituent):
• Base name 'benzene' with the substituent as prefix: chlorobenzene, nitrobenzene, methyl benzene.
• Many have common names accepted by IUPAC as base names: phenol (C₆H₅OH), toluene (C₆H₅CH₃), aniline (C₆H₅NH₂); special names such as benzene carboxylic acid and benzene sulphonic acid.
• The substituent is always at C-1, so no number is needed.

Disubstituted benzenes (two substituents):
• The carbon with the higher-priority substituent is C₁; the others are numbered accordingly. Priority: –COOH > –CN > –CHO > –COCH₃ > –OH > –NH₂ > –OR > –R.
• If both have the same priority, the substituent earlier in the alphabet gets C₁, e.g. 1-bromo-3-chlorobenzene.
• Example: –OH with –NH₂ at C₃ gives 3-aminophenol.

Ortho, meta, para: for two substituents, ortho (o-) = 1,2; meta (m-) = 1,3; para (p-) = 1,4. E.g. 1,4-dibromobenzene = p-dibromobenzene.

book_ref.quote: We will look into nomenclature of monocyclic aromatic compounds first.

blocks.prompt: 6 Compare the reactivity of benzene with that of alkanes and alkenes. Why does benzene undergo electrophilic substitution rather than addition? (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Alkanes: generally unreactive because they are non-polar and have only σ bonds; they undergo free radical substitution quite easily in UV light.

Alkenes: very reactive because of the π bond and π electrons available to electrophiles; they undergo electrophilic addition easily, e.g. cyclohexene adds bromine readily without a catalyst.

Benzene: has three π bonds and, like alkenes, reacts with electrophiles, but with two key differences:
• it is very stable, so less reactive (it needs a Lewis acid to react with Br₂ or Cl₂);
• it undergoes electrophilic substitution, not addition: C₆H₆ + Br₂ → (FeBr₃) C₆H₅Br + HBr.

Reason: the aromatic ring is stabilised by extensive delocalisation of π electrons. In substitution the aromaticity is broken in the intermediate but restored at the end, so the ring's stability is kept. In addition the delocalisation would be destroyed, so addition is not favourable.

book_ref.quote: However, there are two key differences between their reactions with electrophiles:

rows: React with Br₂ only with a Lewis acid

blocks.prompt: 7 Describe the general mechanism of electrophilic aromatic substitution. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Whatever the electrophile, the mechanism has three main steps.

Step 1, generation of the electrophile: the electrophile (E⁺) is a positive ion or the positive end of a polar molecule. It usually cannot simply be added, so it is produced in situ by adding suitable reagents, e.g. Br₂ + AlBr₃ → Br⁺ + [AlBr₄]⁻.

Step 2, electrophilic attack: the π electrons of benzene attack E⁺, forming a σ bond between one ring carbon and E. This carbon becomes sp³. Aromaticity is disrupted: only four π electrons remain and the positive charge is spread over five carbon atoms. Because of the new σ bond, the intermediate is called a sigma complex (arenium ion).
C₆H₆ + E⁺ → [C₆H₆E]⁺

Step 3, restoration of aromaticity: a counterion/conjugate base removes the H from the sp³ carbon by heterolytic cleavage of the C–H bond. The bonding electrons go back into the π system and delocalisation is restored.
[C₆H₆E]⁺ → C₆H₅E + H⁺

Overall a hydrogen of the ring is replaced by the electrophile, and the stable aromatic ring is kept.

book_ref.quote: Regardless of electrophile used, the electrophilic aromatic substitution mechanism can be divided into three main steps.

blocks.prompt: 8 Describe the bromination of benzene in the presence of AlBr₃, giving the mechanism and the role of the Lewis acid. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Benzene reacts with bromine only in the presence of a Lewis acid (AlCl₃, FeCl₃ or FeBr₃, here AlBr₃), which coordinates to the halogen and generates a strong electrophile.
Overall: C₆H₆ + Br₂ → (AlBr₃) C₆H₅Br + HBr

Mechanism:
1. Formation of the electrophile: AlBr₃ polarises Br₂ (Brδ+–Brδ−) and takes Br⁻:
Br₂ + AlBr₃ → Br⁺ + [AlBr₄]⁻
2. Attack of Br⁺: the π electrons of the ring attack Br⁺, forming the sigma complex [C₆H₆Br]⁺; aromaticity is temporarily lost.
3. Loss of the proton: [AlBr₄]⁻ removes H⁺ from the sp³ carbon; aromaticity is restored and the catalyst is regenerated:
[C₆H₆Br]⁺ + [AlBr₄]⁻ → C₆H₅Br + HBr + AlBr₃

Role of the Lewis acid: it generates Br⁺ and is regenerated at the end, so it acts as a catalyst. In the same way FeCl₃ generates Cl⁺ for chlorination, with an identical mechanism.

blocks.prompt: 9 Describe the nitration of benzene, giving the reagents, conditions, mechanism and the effect of temperature. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Nitration introduces a nitro group on benzene using a mixture of conc. HNO₃ and conc. H₂SO₄.
C₆H₆ + HNO₃ → (conc. H₂SO₄) C₆H₅NO₂ + H₂O

Mechanism:
1. Generation of the electrophile: the NO₂⁺ ion is generated by reacting conc. HNO₃ with conc. H₂SO₄.
2. Electrophilic attack: a pair of electrons from the benzene ring is donated to NO₂⁺, forming a covalent bond and the sigma complex; aromaticity is lost.
3. Restoration of aromaticity: the C–H bond of the substituted carbon breaks and its electrons go back into the π system, giving nitrobenzene.

Role of H₂SO₄: it acts as a catalyst, so it is not written in the equation.

Effect of temperature: at higher temperatures there is a greater chance of more than one nitro group being substituted. A certain amount of 1,3-dinitrobenzene forms even at 50 °C, because –NO₂ is a meta director.

blocks.prompt: 10 Describe Friedel-Crafts alkylation of benzene with its three-step mechanism, taking chloroethane as the alkyl halide. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
In Friedel-Crafts alkylation an alkyl group is substituted into the benzene ring in the presence of the Lewis acid AlCl₃.
Overall: C₆H₆ + CH₃CH₂Cl → (AlCl₃) C₆H₅CH₂CH₃ + HCl

Step 1, formation of the carbocation: AlCl₃ reacts with the alkyl halide, forming a carbocation which acts as the electrophile:
CH₃CH₂Cl + AlCl₃ → CH₃CH₂⁺ + AlCl₄⁻

Step 2, attack on the carbocation: the π electrons of the ring attack the carbocation, forming an arenium ion intermediate. Aromaticity is temporarily lost:
C₆H₆ + CH₃CH₂⁺ → [C₆H₆CH₂CH₃]⁺

Step 3, deprotonation: loss of H⁺ restores aromaticity. The proton forms HCl and AlCl₃ is regenerated:
[C₆H₆CH₂CH₃]⁺ + AlCl₄⁻ → C₆H₅CH₂CH₃ + HCl + AlCl₃

AlCl₃ is regenerated, so it is a catalyst; the product is ethylbenzene, an alkylbenzene.

book_ref.quote: The Lewis acid catalyst (AlCl₃) undergoes reaction with the alkyl halide

blocks.prompt: 11 What is an acyl group? Describe Friedel-Crafts acylation of benzene with its mechanism, taking propanoyl chloride, CH₃CH₂COCl, as the acyl halide. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
An acyl group is an alkyl group attached to a carbonyl group, R–C=O. In Friedel-Crafts acylation an acyl group is substituted into the benzene ring in the presence of the Lewis acid AlCl₃.
Overall: C₆H₆ + CH₃CH₂COCl → (AlCl₃) C₆H₅COCH₂CH₃ + HCl

Mechanism:
1. Formation of the acylium ion: AlCl₃ forms a complex with the acyl halide, which loses a halide ion:
CH₃CH₂COCl + AlCl₃ → CH₃CH₂CO⁺ + AlCl₄⁻
2. Electrophilic attack: the π electrons of the ring attack the acylium ion (RCO⁺), giving the intermediate complex (sigma complex).
3. Deprotonation: the intermediate loses H⁺, restoring aromaticity.
4. The proton attaches to a chloride ion forming HCl, and AlCl₃ is regenerated:
H⁺ + AlCl₄⁻ → HCl + AlCl₃

The product is an acyl benzene, C₆H₅COCH₂CH₃.

book_ref.quote: A reaction occurs between the Lewis acid catalyst (AlCl₃) and the acyl halide.

blocks.prompt: 12 Explain how the electrophile is generated in (i) bromination (ii) nitration (iii) Friedel-Crafts alkylation (iv) Friedel-Crafts acylation of benzene. Name the electrophile and the product in each case. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
In every electrophilic substitution the first step generates the electrophile in situ from suitable reagents; the rest of the mechanism (attack, sigma complex, loss of H⁺) is the same.

(i) Bromination: Br₂ with a Lewis acid (AlBr₃/FeBr₃): Br₂ + AlBr₃ → Br⁺ + [AlBr₄]⁻. Electrophile Br⁺; product bromobenzene, C₆H₅Br.
(ii) Nitration: conc. HNO₃ with conc. H₂SO₄ generates NO₂⁺. Electrophile NO₂⁺; product nitrobenzene, C₆H₅NO₂.
(iii) Alkylation: alkyl halide with AlCl₃: RCl + AlCl₃ → R⁺ + AlCl₄⁻. Electrophile carbocation R⁺; product alkylbenzene, C₆H₅R.
(iv) Acylation: acyl halide with AlCl₃: RCOCl + AlCl₃ → RCO⁺ + AlCl₄⁻. Electrophile acylium ion RCO⁺; product acyl benzene, C₆H₅COR.

In each case the catalyst (Lewis acid or H₂SO₄) is regenerated.

book_ref.quote: Generation of electrophile: The first step of an electrophilic substitution reaction involves the generation of an electrophile.

blocks.prompt: 13 What are meta-directing groups? Explain their effect on the reactivity of the ring and on orientation, with examples and the chlorination of nitrobenzene. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Any group attached to the benzene ring affects further electrophilic substitution and decides the orientation of the incoming electrophile.

Meta-directing (deactivating) groups:
• A group that makes the ring less reactive than benzene and directs the incoming electrophile to the meta position is a meta director.
• Such groups are mostly electron-withdrawing; they destabilize the arenium (sigma complex) intermediate.
• They give mainly the meta (1,3) product.
• Examples: –CN, C=O, –NO₂, –CO₂–.

Example, chlorination of nitrobenzene: –NO₂ is a meta director, so chlorination occurs at the meta position and the major product is 1-chloro-3-nitrobenzene:
C₆H₅NO₂ + Cl₂ → (FeCl₃) m-ClC₆H₄NO₂ + HCl

Similarly, further nitration of nitrobenzene gives 1,3-dinitrobenzene.

book_ref.quote: These substituents direct the reaction to give primarily the

blocks.prompt: 14 What are ortho-para directing groups? Explain with examples, and describe the ring chlorination of methylbenzene with conditions and a balanced equation. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Ortho-para directing (activating) groups:
• A group that makes the ring more reactive than benzene and directs the incoming electrophile to the ortho and para positions is an ortho-para director.
• It gives the ortho (1,2) or para (1,4) product, with a slight preference for para; the meta product is an extremely minor byproduct.
• These groups can donate electrons to the benzene ring.
• Examples: –SR, –R, –OH, –OR, –NR₂, –SH.

Chlorination of methylbenzene:
• Conditions: AlCl₃ (or AlBr₃ with bromine) or iron, absence of UV light, room temperature.
• The methyl group is 2,4-directing, so a mixture of 2-chloromethylbenzene and 4-chloromethylbenzene forms:
2C₆H₅CH₃ + 2Cl₂ → 2-ClC₆H₄CH₃ + 4-ClC₆H₄CH₃ + 2HCl
• With bromine the equivalent bromine compounds form.

Like CH₃, the OH group is a ring activator; in phenol incoming groups go to the 2, 4 and 6 positions.

book_ref.quote: The chlorination in the methyl benzene ring takes place in the presence of aluminium chloride

blocks.prompt: 15 15.6 g of benzene is burnt completely in excess air according to 2C₆H₆ + 15O₂ → 12CO₂ + 6H₂O. Taking C₆H₆ = 78, O₂ = 32, CO₂ = 44 and H₂O = 18 g mol⁻¹, calculate (i) the mass of oxygen used (ii) the masses of CO₂ and H₂O formed, and show that mass is conserved. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation: Convert benzene to moles, then use the mole ratio 2 : 15 : 12 : 6 from the balanced equation.

book_ref.quote: When benzene is burnt in excess of air

steps: Reactants: 15.6 + 48.0 = 63.6 g; products: 52.8 + 10.8 = 63.6 g, so mass is conserved
blocks.final_answer: (i) 48.0 g O₂ (ii) 52.8 g CO₂ and 10.8 g H₂O; total 63.6 g on both sides

blocks.prompt: 16 What is side-chain oxidation of alkylbenzenes? Give the reagents, the condition needed, examples, and its use as an identification test. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Definition: oxidation that takes place at an alkyl group directly attached to a benzene ring is side-chain oxidation.

Reagents: alkaline KMnO₄, acidic K₂Cr₂O₇ or dilute HNO₃.

Product: the alkyl group is oxidized to a carboxylic acid group, regardless of its size, keeping the ring intact. Whatever the length of the alkyl group, only one –COOH is formed per side chain.
• Methylbenzene (toluene) → benzoic acid, C₆H₅COOH.
• Ethylbenzene → benzoic acid.
• An arene with three alkyl groups at 1, 3, 5, each with benzylic H → benzene-1,3,5-tricarboxylic acid.

Condition: at least one benzylic hydrogen must be attached to the carbon next to the ring. With no benzylic H (a tertiary carbon attached to the ring, e.g. tert-butylbenzene) no reaction occurs.

Reason: alkanes and benzene are each very stable to oxidation, but together the benzylic carbon becomes more reactive and susceptible to oxidation.

Identification test: the purple colour of KMnO₄ is discharged when it oxidizes an alkylbenzene with benzylic hydrogen. Benzene and alkylbenzenes with a tertiary alkyl group leave the colour; those with primary or secondary alkyl groups discharge it (the test cannot tell primary from secondary).

book_ref.quote: Following example demonstrates the utilization of oxidation reaction in the production of substituted benzoic acid.

blocks.prompt: 17 Describe the addition reactions of benzene: hydrogenation and addition of halogens. Why do these reactions need special conditions? (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
(a) Hydrogenation: 1, 2 or 3 moles of H₂ add to the carbons of benzene. Complete hydrogenation gives cyclohexane, a useful solvent and a precursor for other chemicals:
C₆H₆ + 3H₂ → (Ni, about 150 °C, high pressure) C₆H₁₂
Methylbenzene similarly gives methylcyclohexane: C₆H₅CH₃ + 3H₂ → C₆H₁₁CH₃.
Conditions: the same finely divided nickel catalyst and similar temperature (around 150 °C) as for alkenes, but a higher pressure.

(b) Addition of halogens: chlorine and bromine react in the same way. Without a catalyst, UV light and heat are sufficient for complete halogenation:
C₆H₆ + 3Cl₂ → (UV light, heat) C₆H₆Cl₆

Why special conditions: these reactions destroy the delocalisation of the benzene ring, because the π electrons are used to form bonds with the new atoms. The reactions are exothermic overall because of the strong new C–H bonds, but there is a high activation barrier, so a higher pressure (hydrogenation) or UV light and heat (halogenation) are needed.

book_ref.quote: We will examine hydrogenation and halogenation addition reactions of benzene in the following reactions.

blocks.prompt: 18 31.2 g of benzene is completely hydrogenated to cyclohexane over a nickel catalyst. Taking C₆H₆ = 78, H₂ = 2 and C₆H₁₂ = 84 g mol⁻¹ and the heat of hydrogenation of benzene from the chapter (208 kJ mol⁻¹ released), calculate (i) the mass of hydrogen needed (ii) the mass of cyclohexane formed (iii) the heat released. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation: Find moles of benzene; use C₆H₆ + 3H₂ → C₆H₁₂ for the masses and 208 kJ per mole of benzene for the heat.

book_ref.quote: Cyclohexane is produced when benzene is completely hydrogenated.

steps: C₆H₆ + 3H₂ → C₆H₁₂: H₂ = 3 × 0.400 = 1.20 mol; mass = 1.20 × 2 = 2.40 g
blocks.final_answer: (i) 2.40 g H₂ (ii) 33.6 g cyclohexane (iii) 83.2 kJ released

blocks.prompt: 19 Benzene reacts with chlorine in two different ways depending on the conditions. Describe (i) the reaction in the presence of FeCl₃ (ii) the reaction in UV light and heat without a catalyst. Explain why the two products differ. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
(i) With FeCl₃ (Lewis acid): electrophilic substitution. FeCl₃ generates Cl⁺, which attacks the π electrons forming a sigma complex; loss of H⁺ restores aromaticity.
C₆H₆ + Cl₂ → (FeCl₃) C₆H₅Cl + HCl
One Cl replaces one H and the aromatic ring is kept.

(ii) In UV light and heat, no catalyst: addition. UV light and heat are sufficient for complete halogenation; three Cl₂ molecules add to the ring.
C₆H₆ + 3Cl₂ → (UV light, heat) C₆H₆Cl₆
The delocalisation is destroyed because the π electrons form bonds with the new chlorine atoms.

Why they differ: with a Lewis acid a strong electrophile is formed and the stable aromatic ring is restored at the end, so substitution is favoured. Under UV light and heat the forcing conditions overcome the high barrier to addition, and the ring's delocalisation is lost.

book_ref.quote: Chlorine and bromine react in the same way.
